Allege

uh-LEJ -- two syllables, stress on the second syllable, LEJ; rhymes with 'edge.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To allege to claim wrongdoing without proof.

The lawsuit alleges that the company knew about the faulty brakes for years.

Worked Example

The school paper's big story says a rival school 'took' the missing mascot costume. The journalism adviser circles the word and hands back the draft: 'You don't know that yet. Write that students allege the costume was taken -- until there's proof, it is an accusation, not a fact.'

The adviser is teaching the exact job of allege: to report a claim of wrongdoing that has not been proven. Newspapers and courts lean on this word -- 'the suspect allegedly...' -- because it draws a bright line between what someone accuses and what anyone has established as true.

How Allege Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

claim

claim: to state something is true without proving it

contend

contend: to argue that something is the case

charge

charge: to accuse someone formally

Antonyms

prove

prove: to establish as true with evidence

retract

retract: to take back a statement

How Strong Is It? — claim → allege → charge

claim vs. allege

claim vs. allege: Claim is the everyday word for any unproven statement, wrongdoing or not -- you can claim you finished your homework.

charge vs. allege

charge vs. allege: Charge is the strongest and most formal: to allege is to raise an unproven accusation, but to charge someone is to accuse them officially, with paperwork and consequences attached.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — al-

prefix — al-: to, toward (a form of ad-) (Latin)

root — lege

root — lege: to send, to commission, to put forward (Latin legare)

Put it together

Put it together: Allege has one of English's most tangled histories: it reached us through an Old French verb that got blended with Latin allegare, 'to put forward, to bring as evidence' -- ad- ('toward') plus legare ('to send, to commission'). The Latin sense won: to allege is to put forward a claim -- to send it into the argument -- while the proof still waits outside. Because two different verbs merged along the way, the exact path is marked uncertain.

Use the root in a new word: delegate

Use the root in a new word: delegate: The principal delegated the morning announcements to the vice principal.

Root Check

Word Choice

Allege lives in legal and journalistic writing, and it always signals an unproven accusation: reports allege, lawsuits allege, witnesses allege. You met its noun cousin earlier in this course -- Allegations, from the Part 2 catch-all unit: an allegation is exactly what someone who alleges produces. And keep allege apart from its unit-mate affirm: to affirm is to state a fact you stand behind; to allege is to raise a claim no one has yet proven.
